Girolamo Doria (unknown – 1558) was an Italian Roman Catholic cardinal who played a significant role in the Counter-Reformation. As a member of the College of Cardinals, he participated in the election of Pope Paul IV in 1555 and later served as papal legate to the Holy Roman Empire. Doria's tenure as cardinal coincided with the tumultuous events of the Italian Wars, including the Siege of Florence (1527) and the Sack of Rome (1526). His involvement with the papacy was also marked by controversy, particularly during the reign of Pope Pius IV.

Doria's legacy extends beyond his own lifetime, as he contributed to the development of the Catholic Church's response to Protestantism. His experiences as a cardinal shaped his understanding of the complex dynamics between church and state, influencing the course of European politics for centuries to come.

One striking statistic from Doria's life is his involvement in the Inquisition, which he participated in during his time as papal legate. This episode highlights the darker aspects of religious authority during the Renaissance period.

In conclusion, Girolamo Doria's significance lies not only in his own historical context but also in the broader cultural and political landscape of 16th-century Europe.
